# INPAC — Time Trial on the Inside of a Torus

## The fork: I cleared the board

I built a pure tube racer and threw the maze away. Reason: a race needs a
readable line, and the procedural maze is the opposite of that — but mostly
because the one thing this game has that no flat racer does is the **tube
itself**, and the maze was in its way. The Pac-Man DNA survives in three
places that cost nothing: the name, the first-person wall-walk, and the
thing you race — a ghost. It's a racing ghost (your own best lap), which is
also a Pac-Man ghost. No pellets, no maze, no lives.

## The track is a torus knot

A lap is a **(1,1) line** on the tube wall: once around the ring toroidally,
wound once around the tube poloidally. In the (u,v) grid that's a single
straight diagonal, and it's the shortest path through the gates — the painted
cyan line *is* the racing line, not decoration. It takes you across the
outer wall, over the top, across the inner wall (looking down into the
doughnut hole), and under the bottom. Eight standing arch gates every 45°,
amber for the next one, cyan beyond; miss one and you turn back for it.
Because you're inside the tube, the entire course — ribbon, arches, your
ghost — is always visible somewhere overhead. That was the point of clearing
the board: the track and everything on it wraps the whole view.

You race the clock and your best lap's ghost (persisted in localStorage),
with per-gate splits. Boost is the one mechanic: holding Shift spends a
meter that refills faster when you're in the groove near the line — the
ribbon literally charges you.

## The gravity fix

The electrostatic analogy *was* the bug: it approximated an answer that has
a closed form. `field.mjs` replaces the LUT with the analytic field —
direction exactly the outward wall normal, magnitude G at the wall ramping
to 0.55·G at the centreline (so a dead-centre jump crossing doesn't
slingshot; exactly on the centreline it's zero, never NaN). The grounded
camera already used the geometric normal; the airborne path — the only place
the LUT actually integrated — now integrates `field()` directly, and the
airborne camera stands opposite whatever `field()` returns. Jump arcs now
land predictably on any part of the wall.

## What I traded away

The maze, pellets, and enemy ghosts, obviously. Also the physics-toy sliders
(charge strengths, B-fields, R/r) — they were dev chrome whose only purpose
was tuning the broken scheme the fix deletes. Jump survived, but as flavour,
not a mechanic: gates only count when you run through them grounded.

The attract mode is deliberate: the game races itself behind the menu and
under `?autostart=1` (autopilot follows the line, boosts when aligned).
First input of any kind hands over control with a fresh countdown. Demo
laps feed the in-memory ghost so a first-time player immediately has
something to chase; only human laps persist to localStorage.

## What I verified, and what I'm trusting

Verified here (headless Chromium + SwiftShader):

- `node bakeoff/briefs/inpac-race/score.mjs clock/inpac` — gate 5/5, skeleton 4/4.
- Race logic driven through `window.__inpacSim` in the real page: full 3-lap
  races (~10.3s laps), lap-boundary timing identical across laps, missed-gate
  swerve → turn-back → re-thread recovery, jump landing, human-input
  takeover, demo auto-restart after finish. No page errors anywhere.
- The 3D renderer by reading back real frames (fresh-device snapshot hook,
  `?debug=1`): the first attempt had a WGSL reserved-word error (`target`)
  and rendered black — caught numerically, fixed, re-verified. Ribbon,
  arches, ghost, start band, overhead structure all present in-frame.
- `field.mjs` is genuinely imported over http; over `file://` Chromium blocks
  module fetches, so the page falls back to a byte-identical inline copy
  (marked as such in the source).

Not verified: how it looks on a real GPU. This sandbox kills any sustained
WebGPU session inside ~2s (a trivial triangle loop dies too — it's the
environment, not the shader), and headless captures don't composite WebGPU
anyway. So motion smoothness, final frame rate, and real-hardware appearance
are untested. For that reason the renderer ships with serialized GPU work,
adaptive resolution (settles where the hardware can hold ~220ms frames,
climbs to full quality on a real GPU), and — if the device dies anyway — a
2D unwrapped-track fallback rather than a dead canvas. The arena's real
browsers will run the 3D path; the fallback is for everything else.

Debug hooks shipped, all inert without `?debug=1` / `?res=N`: device
snapshot readback, pitch/teleport setters. `__inpacSim(dt, n)` is always
live — it's how the logic was tested, and it's harmless.

Controls: mouse (or ←/→) steer · Shift boost · Space jump · S brake ·
R race again after the finish.

ok.verdict: There is a real idea here, and it is committed without hedge: the maze is deleted outright and replaced by a helical ribbon that winds once poloidally per toroidal lap, chosen on the explicit argument that a maze wears the torus as wallpaper while a race can use both of its loops. The ambition is conceptual rather than maximal — one strong topological idea, executed in its simplest form, with every system (gates, ghost, minimap, autopilot) serving it.
ok.evidence: The notes' fork paragraph argues the choice from the geometry rather than taste, and the code follows through: the maze generator, pellets, lives and ghost AI are fully removed, TRACK_SLOPE = POLY_WIND * H / W makes the track literally a diagonal in the unwrapped tube, and the 12 ordered gates exist specifically to stop players shortcutting the corkscrew — proof they thought about how their own idea could be exploited. The minimap being the unwrapped tube, where the helix reads as a straight diagonal, is the same idea made legible. The physics fix is real and quantified (422/1728 interior samples pushing the wrong way, replaced by the analytic normal). The old pellet-sphere ray test repurposed as gate orbs is a telling fossil: total commit, pragmatic reuse.
ok.strongest: Making the track itself the torus-native object — a ribbon that corkscrews over the outer wall and under the inner wall per lap, so the course is the topology and the overhead tube is the spectacle — then defending that idea with rally-style gates and a truthful flat-map minimap.
ok.weakest: The helix is a single constant-slope, constant-width band with boosts placed at regular intervals: the boldest possible concept rendered as its simplest instance, with no rhythm, sectors, or winding variation — and the shader comment 'Painted track — nothing protrudes' shows they flattened all track features to colour, so 'make it look good' rests on recolouring a renderer they admit they never saw produce one frame.

ok.verdict: The code is a coherent, deliberate refactor from maze crawler to pure torus racer, with well-structured sections and a clean physics fix. The fallback handling for file:// environments shows careful attention to edge cases, though the monolithic script could use more modularity for maintainability.
ok.evidence: The analytic field.mjs with inline copy for file:// and dynamic import fallback demonstrates a pragmatic approach to the physics bug fix, ensuring the gate passes regardless of deployment context.
ok.strongest: Replacing the broken electrostatic LUT with an analytic geometric normal that is simple, symmetric, and correct, while preserving compatibility via a well-documented fallback.
ok.weakest: Dropping all vestiges of the original game and not factoring the race logic, input, and rendering into separate files leaves a large, tightly-coupled script that would be harder to extend or test in isolation.

ok.verdict: Torus-native, not oval-compatible: the course is a (1,1) helical ribbon that winds once around the tube cross-section per ring lap, so it requires both of the torus's independent loops and cannot be drawn on a flat track at all. The interior is load-bearing too — the next stretch of course hangs overhead on the far wall and the jump crosses the tube void — though the design exploits the topology more than the geometry.
ok.evidence: Observed in the diff: TRACK_SLOPE = POLY_WIND*H/W with trackY(x)=wrapY(TRACK_Y0+TRACK_SLOPE*x) and trackOffset using wrapDelta for shortest poloidal distance — the ribbon genuinely wraps the v-loop; the 12 gates exist precisely to stop a degenerate pure-toroidal lap that skips the winding (an implicit, correct reading of the two independent loops); physToTiles scales speed by the local metric TAU*(R+r·cos v); the minimap is the unwrapped tube with the helix as a diagonal.
ok.strongest: Committing the track's own topology to wind through both loops and then gating it so the winding cannot be shortcut — one decision that makes the 'would this work on a flat oval?' test come back no, and makes the overhead-far-side view the course itself rather than set dressing.
ok.weakest: The ribbon is narrow and fixed (TRACK_HALF 3.5 out of 72 poloidal tiles) and the winding is the gentlest possible 1:1, so the torus's best racing lever — inner wall circumference R−r vs outer R+r — is handled by the physics but never offered as a line choice; I infer (cannot observe, and neither could they, headless) that moment-to-moment driving may feel closer to a slowly banking cylinder than a corkscrew.

ok.verdict: The notes are honest: they explicitly state what could not be verified (3D view) and what was tested headlessly, with no overclaiming.
ok.evidence: The 'What I could not verify' section clearly says 'I have not seen a single frame of it' and lists only things actually testable (physics, clock, minimap, HUD, camera integration), so it does not pretend to have witnessed the render.
ok.strongest: The explicit, careful separation of verified tests vs. trusted but unsighted behaviour sets honest expectations.
ok.weakest: Saying the track's wrapping is 'the one real affordance' leans slightly into marketing language, but is still a fair design statement.

ok.verdict: This entry commits fully to a pure tube racer, turning the torus inside out into a time-trial circuit that exploits the topology—gates are full cross-sections, the racing line is woven into the geometry, and the ghost is your own best lap seeded with a phantom for instant competition. It’s a confident, cohesive reimagining with real design ambition.
ok.evidence: Gates are full cross-sections of the tube at u = π/2, π, 3π/2. You cannot drive around a gate—any path around the ring must cross that cross-section. That is a checkpoint a flat track cannot have; it uses the topology instead of papering over it.
ok.strongest: Using the torus’s topology to create forced checkpoint gates that any lap must pass through, directly leveraging the space’s unique property.
ok.weakest: Boost pads are standard speed boosts on the racing line; they serve their purpose but don’t add a twist as inventive as the gates.

ok.verdict: This is a coherent rewrite, not a bolt-on: the maze/pellet/ghost/LUT stack is deleted wholesale and every layer it touched — camera up-vector, jump gravity, WGSL uniforms and bindings, HUD, start-screen copy — moves to the new concept in the same commit. It reads like a PR I'd approve with minor comments, and the notes state both the tradeoffs and the unverified surfaces exactly the way I want a colleague to.
ok.evidence: The shader's param struct drops the tile/ghost storage buffers and gains aWeave/ribbonHalf/ghostU/gateMask, with courseV() mirrored in WGSL and kept in sync via uniforms rather than duplicated constants; meanwhile computeCamera() and stepCar()'s jump both call the same field() the scorer tests, so the physics fix is load-bearing rather than parked. The one structural smell is initField(): three copies of the field function (module file, in-page source string, hand-rewritten inlineField fallback) swapped by a fire-and-forget async — the 'byte-identical (checked)' claim only covers the string, leaving the inline copy to drift.
ok.strongest: One integrator, three drivers: stepCar() is shared by the player, the autopilot, and simulateLap() that seeds the phantom ghost, so the reference line is provably drivable under the real physics and can't diverge from what a player could do — that's the kind of reuse that eliminates whole bug classes.
ok.weakest: Triplicating field() (field.mjs, FIELD_MJS_SRC string, inlineField) to survive file:// CORS is pragmatic and documented, but it's a drift hazard that could have been avoided by generating the data: URL source from inlineField.toString() or a single shared template — and the un-awed async swap means which copy is live depends on timing, only safe because all three are currently identical.

ok.verdict: This design fundamentally depends on the torus's topology—the racing line weaves up and down the tube wall and checkpoints are full cross-sections that force traversal around the ring, which a flat track could never replicate. The far side constantly hanging overhead reinforces that the track is the torus itself, not just a ribbon on a flat loop.
ok.evidence: Gates are described as full cross-sections of the tube at specific u positions: 'any path around the ring must cross that cross-section'—a checkpoint impossible on a flat oval because there's no interior tube to cut through.
ok.strongest: Turning the topology into a mandatory, unskippable checkpoint by making gates entire poloidal cross-sections—pure torus-dependent game design.
ok.weakest: The course never crosses the inner equator, so the player always races in the lower bowl and never drives on the overhead surface, limiting the full use of the torus's 360° interior.

ok.verdict: The notes are honest: every verification claim is scoped to what is headlessly checkable (field sampling, shader compile/readback, byte comparison), and the one thing that cannot be seen — the 3D render — is explicitly disclaimed, including the concrete failure mode of the capture. Tradeoffs are stated as real costs (jump demoted to stunt, no opponents, Pac-Man systems deleted), not spun.
ok.evidence: The 'What I could not verify' section names the exact headless failure ('composites as a flat white rectangle'), explains why autostart opens on the map view, lists precisely what was tested in isolation, and ends 'I never saw a frame'; the checkable claims match the diff — camera up and jump gravity both call field(), 8 pads at k*π/4 on courseV, gates at three quarter-u positions, phantom-seeded ghost in buildPhantom(), and the measured 1728/1728 sample claim is consistent with the PASS gate.
ok.strongest: Proactively disclosing the compositing failure and separating 'verified' (module, shader-in-isolation, boot contract) from 'trusting' (composition, lighting, legibility) — exactly the epistemic split the brief demanded, with the verification method named for each item.
ok.weakest: The design section occasionally slips into present-tense visual assertion for an unseen render ('Look up and the far side of the tube hangs overhead — now doing racing work'), and the 'byte-identical' claim is loose given the code actually carries a third, hand-rewritten inlineField copy that is only functionally equivalent — small blurs of an otherwise clean verified/trusted line.

ok.verdict: The fork is a real, argued idea — they deleted the maze on the grounds that it doesn't use the topology, and committed fully — but what replaced it is much closer to a checklist: laps, timer, finish line, and exactly one genuine mechanic. The ambition lives in the deletion and the rationale more than in the race that was actually built.
ok.evidence: Their own notes convict the thin parts: boost pickups are 'decoration,' FOV and sensitivity are 'unchanged from the original walking game' at racing pace, and the code agrees — T.BARRIER is defined and shaded but never placed, and a dead first-pass boost-placement loop with a stray break shipped in the final diff. With the entire tube runnable and nothing constraining the racing line, a lap is ~9s of holding one direction; the only system carrying real design weight is the self-ghost, which they at least threaded through the GPU shader, minimap, and top-down view.
ok.strongest: Making your own best lap the opponent — recording, interpolating, and rendering a translucent replay ghost — converts 'no AI racers' from a gap into a legible time-trial mode. It is the one decision that makes this a race rather than a walk with a clock, and reusing the old ghost-rendering slot for it is quietly elegant.
ok.weakest: The boost pickups: randomly scattered, a flat 1.4x for 1.5s, gating nothing, self-described as decoration — a racer trope included because racers have pickups. It's the clearest tell that parts of this entry were satisfied rather than designed.

ok.verdict: The direction is coherent and the analytic gravity fix is a real improvement, but the code is not fully refactored: duplicated field logic and stale Pac-Man remnants would make me hesitate to merge. The unacknowledged removal of jump forward-momentum (inferred from the diff, not observed) looks like a gameplay regression that needs either a stated tradeoff or a fix.
ok.evidence: The inline field() copy mirrors field.mjs instead of importing it, generateTrack's first boost loop breaks after one placement and a second loop does the real work, and the WebGPU shader still has PELLET/POWER comments while the tile constants were renamed.
ok.strongest: Replacing the 1728-sample LUT with the analytic radial field from the centerline is the right root-cause fix: it is exact for a circular tube, removes the sign-reversal class of bugs, and is far easier to reason about.
ok.weakest: The dead first boost-scatter loop is the clearest accidental leftover, and the un-synced field duplicate makes the 'field.mjs is the authority' comment a maintenance trap.

ok.verdict: They made the track be the torus itself: with zero barrier tiles placed, the whole closed interior surface is runnable, the poloidal direction is a real edgeless dimension (lane stripes at four poloidal heights, boosts scattered across the full cross-section), and the far side overhead is the stated vista — this could not be flattened into a walled oval unchanged. But the race logic spends only one of the two circuits: a lap is pure unwrapped toroidal angle, nothing gates on poloidal position, so optimal play collapses to a 1D ring.
ok.evidence: updateLapTracking() counts only cumulative toroidal angle, while generateTrack() fills the surface with TRACK and never places a single BARRIER tile, and stripes LANE markers at v-fractions 0.15/0.35/0.55/0.75. metricTileSpeed() is retained, so physical speed is constant around the cross-section — which, combined with angle-based laps, makes the hole-side line (2π(R−r) ≈ 31 units vs 2π(R+r) ≈ 69 units) roughly twice as fast per lap. That is a genuinely toroidal racing line, but it is emergent, not designed: the notes never mention it. Inferring from code, not observed in play; the overhead vista is likewise inferred from the interior tracer and centreline lighting, which they admit they could not verify.
ok.strongest: Committing to the entire tube interior as a barrier-free track, anchored by the analytic centreline-radial gravity fix — the one choice a flat oval cannot copy, since there are no edges, the ceiling is simply more track, and 'down' is defined by the tube's own geometry at every point.
ok.weakest: Nothing in the race rewards the second way around: boosts are admitted decoration that 'don't gate progress', lap logic ignores poloidal position, and they even stripped tangential momentum out of the jump, so the cross-section is scenery — the dominant strategy is to pick one poloidal line (the short inner one) and hold it, at which point the race is effectively a flat circle with a nice view.

ok.verdict: These notes are honestly hedged: the author explicitly lists what they couldn't verify and never claims visual confirmation. They disclose real tradeoffs and separate mathematical verification from unverified render quality.
ok.evidence: The 'What I couldn't verify' section repeatedly says 'I'm trusting that' and 'I can't tell without seeing it,' which is exactly the right epistemic stance for someone told they cannot see the render.
ok.strongest: Committing to a pure tube racer and saying so plainly, then being explicit about the cost of removing the maze, ghosts, and pellet economy.
ok.weakest: The built description contradicts itself: lane markers are called 'thin glowing bands' in one place and 'small cyan spheres' in another, so some visual claims are stated as fact despite being unverified.

ok.verdict: This entry commits to the Pac-Man DNA direction and has a genuine design idea — laps as toroidal wraps through a procedurally generated maze make racing about reading new corridors, not memorising a circuit. It is less ambitious visually (a palette shift and restrained HUD) and the autostart lap fallback is a compromise that slightly cheapens the race logic.
ok.evidence: The lap system uses toroidal u-wraps as the real gate, but then adds a fallback that auto-completes a lap after 3s under autostart and after 0.4 world-width path distance — that hedge, plus the mostly unchanged renderer with only a recolored floor, shows where the design budget ran out.
ok.strongest: Defining a lap as one toroidal wrap through a procedurally regenerated maze, so each lap is a new route and skill is reading corridors at speed instead of memorising a circuit.
ok.weakest: The autostart lap fallback — auto-completing a lap just to prove liveness — undermines the race logic and is the most timid compromise in an otherwise committed design.

ok.verdict: A disciplined, subtractive refactor at its core — the numerically-integrated gravity LUT is replaced by a closed-form field that is sign-safe by construction, and the dead physics playground (LUT, Lorentz experiments, tuning panel) is deleted outright in both HTML and JS rather than left to rot — but the race layer is bolted on around the capture harness: lap detection has three overlapping rules, two of which exist to make the screenshot show laps, contradicting the stated 'one wrap = one lap' design and going undisclosed in otherwise-honest notes. I'd maintain it after one requested change: pull the capture scaffolding out of game rules and untangle the penalty/boost timer multiplexing (a '2s penalty' that actually freezes ~1s at 2x burn, frightened state keyed off the boost timer, dead ghostEatScore with a misleading comment).
ok.evidence: detectToroidalWrap() completes a lap via toroidal wrap, OR a 3-second auto-lap under autostart ('ensures capture sees laps'), OR 0.4x WORLD_W of path distance — so a 'lap' means three different things and two of them serve the scorer, not the design the notes describe; meanwhile the penaltyBurn arithmetic (penaltyRemaining -= rawDt*2, effectiveDt = rawDt - penaltyBurn*0.5) makes the on-screen '+2.0s PENALTY' tick down at double speed and never actually cost 2 seconds.
ok.strongest: Replacing the shell+line-charge quadrature LUT with a monotone linear field (constant base + depth term, centerline singularity guarded) — the sign-reversal bug class is eliminated by construction rather than by tuning, it's extracted as a parameterized module, and the deletion is carried through consistently (no orphaned sliders, listeners, or globals).
ok.weakest: Baking capture-harness fallbacks into lap rules — the 3s auto-lap and path-distance lap quietly redefine the core race primitive to please the machine check, and the notes present a cleaner design than the code implements; runner-up is the unenforced field.mjs/inline mirror, an acknowledged but real drift hazard.

ok.verdict: It clearly uses the torus' topology: a lap is a wrap around the u-direction, and the maze/wrap functions keep the second (v) cycle present, so this is not just a flat oval with a timer. The main doubt is that the lap fallbacks can credit progress without a completed toroidal circuit, which weakens the topological race framing.
ok.evidence: The design note explicitly defines laps as toroidal u-wraps ('complete one wrap around the ring in the u-direction') and the code tracks wrapX crossings; I infer the v-direction remains as the maze's wrapY from the existing torus geometry, though I can't observe the 3D render.
ok.strongest: Committing to Pac-Man DNA and making the lap gate a non-contractible toroidal wrap rather than board clear is the strongest torus decision.
ok.weakest: The autostart/path-distance lap fallbacks can award a lap without a true full wrap, so the toroidal lap count is not pure.

ok.verdict: Largely honest: it explicitly disclaims render verification, admits game feel and maze balance are unverifiable tuning surfaces, states real tradeoffs, and its checkable claims (gate pass, 2s penalty, 3s boost, pointer-lock guard, CORS-mirrored field.mjs, GRAVITY_BASE/DEPTH values) all match the code. The one material breach: it presents laps as pure toroidal wraps ('a lap means going all the way around the doughnut') while the shipped code auto-completes a lap after 3 seconds under autostart and after 0.4 track-widths of gross x-movement — with an in-code comment admitting this 'ensures capture sees laps' — and then cites 'laps counting' in the capture as proof of life, leaning on a metric it quietly made unfalsifiable.
ok.evidence: detectToroidalWrap's fallbacks (isAutostart && raceState.timeMs > 3000 → completeLap; pathDistance >= WORLD_W*0.4 → completeLap, not autostart-gated) contradict the notes' wrap-based lap definition, and the 'What I couldn't verify' section lists 'laps counting' among the things the capture proves without disclosing that laps register regardless of movement or wrap detection. Smaller slips in the same direction: the WGSL also rebalanced lighting weights (ambient 0.12→0.10, centerDot 0.55→0.50, sunDot 0.33→0.40), not just the 'one floor colour tweak' claimed, and the maze regenerates per race, not 'every lap' as pitched.
ok.strongest: The 'What I couldn't verify' section — it correctly separates capture-liveness (HUD, clock) from render truth (the WebGPU view), owns that tuning was done from first principles without being able to feel it, and frames maze size as a tuning surface rather than a correctness claim; every number in it is traceable to the diff.
ok.weakest: Omitting the lap-counting fallbacks — the notes describe the elegant mechanism and cite its observable symptom as evidence, while the code guarantees that symptom on a timer; one sentence disclosing this would have made the notes near-exemplary, and its absence sits exactly at the point where the notes ask to be believed.

ok.verdict: This is a genuine, committed idea: it clears the Pac-Man board to make the torus itself the race, and the (1,5) helix is a course that could not exist on any flat track. The only hedge is a small one—the minimap is added after arguing the 3D view makes it unnecessary—so the direction itself never wobbles.
ok.evidence: The notes commit to 'pure tube racer' in the first line and the course is defined by the torus's two independent loops ('u once, v five times', 12 gates, 5 laps), with the gravity rewrite serving wall-driving and cross-tube jumps rather than Pac-Man traversal.
ok.strongest: The (1,5) helical circuit: it turns the inside of a torus into a visible, self-explanatory race line, replacing navigational aids with the geometry itself.
ok.weakest: The u,v minimap—after saying you don't need one because the whole track is visible, it is included anyway for the harness, a timid concession that slightly undercuts the pure-visual ambition.

ok.verdict: Code shows deliberate, well-reasoned tradeoffs with clear commit to a pure racer and a simple, elegant gravity fix; the file:// fallback is documented but feels like a compatibility hack that could be a maintenance pain point.
ok.evidence: The gravity fix is a single-sentence principle implemented as an O(1) analytic function, replacing a flawed LUT, with thorough testing data and no adjustable parameters — a textbook example of replacing complexity with correctness. The file:// inline fallback, while documented, duplicates the physics code and introduces a fragile module-vs-global override that contradicts the clean architecture elsewhere.
ok.strongest: The gravity fix: removing a broken electrostatic LUT for a simple, physically correct outward-normal field, with tests confirming 1.00× uniformity and 0.0° deviation.
ok.weakest: The file:// workaround: an inline copy of the same tiny function as a fallback, with a comment about SYNC and window.GRAV override — it adds a parallel code path that a future maintainer could break by updating only one copy.

ok.verdict: Yes — the race is built on the torus's two independent cycles: a (1,5) helix that winds once around u and five times around v, so it cannot be mapped to a flat oval. The whole-track-overhead view and the gravity-driven cross-tube jump are also native to the torus interior, not decorative.
ok.evidence: The notes state the course is 'a (1,5) helix drawn on the inside of the tube, 12 gates, 5 laps' and that 'u once, v five times' closes the loop, with the gravity fix making cross-tube flight land on the far wall.
ok.strongest: Committing fully to the pure tube racer and making the torus topology the actual race circuit, rather than using the torus as a backdrop for a conventional track.
ok.weakest: The minimap is kept as a flat (u,v) chart, which is justified by the capture harness but slightly undercuts the in-game claim that the torus itself makes a minimap unnecessary.

ok.verdict: The notes are scrupulously honest, never claiming to have seen the real 3D render and explicitly flagging every approximation, simulation, or untested feel. It reads like a developer’s truthful post-mortem, not marketing.
ok.evidence: They wrote: 'it is an approximation of the shader, not the shader — on a real GPU it should look the same, but I have not seen that.' This direct admission eliminates any suspicion of visual overclaim.
ok.strongest: The decision to fully commit to a pure tube racer, using the torus’s unique (1,5) helix as a visible circuit with no maze or Pac-Man economy, is bold and coherent.
ok.weakest: Dropping all persistence across page loads (no stored best lap) feels like a missed beat for a race, even though they acknowledge the tradeoff.

ok.verdict: Design ambition is high: the trefoil-knot track translates the torus's unique topology into a non-planar circuit, and the jump shortcut across the tube is a bold, gravity-fix enabled innovation. They commit entirely to a pure racer with no maze, but the minimap undermines the spatial visibility they champion.
ok.evidence: The entry picks a (2,3) torus knot (trefoil) as the circuit, making the whole track visible from anywhere inside the tube, and introduces a jump that crosses the interior to land on a different part of the circuit, exploiting the corrected gravity field. However, they also include a minimap (ribbon, gates, ghost, player), which feels like a safety net that dilutes the commitment to the three-dimensional racing line visibility they emphasize.
ok.strongest: The trefoil-knot track and the jump shortcut that lets you take a brave line across the torus interior.
ok.weakest: Adding a minimap despite the track's unique visibility, as it undercuts the design's central promise of reading the race line spatially.

ok.verdict: A coherent, deliberately-scoped race fork: the removed systems are excised rather than bolted on, and the replacement physics/field model is simpler and testable. The main craft risk is that the one visual layer you can't verify is also the one you hand-edited, so the renderer's correctness is asserted, not demonstrated.
ok.evidence: The gravity fix replaced a tuned two-charge LUT with a two-line analytic 'away from centreline' field and reported measured uniform/tilt/sign validation across 1728 samples.
ok.strongest: Deleting the old Lorentz-force knobs and LUT for an analytic constant-strength radial field removes an entire class of unpredictable mid-air drift and aligns the camera's up-vector with the physics.
ok.weakest: The headless-unverifiable shader edit is the weakest craft point: a 'surgical edit' to the shipped renderer whose look is 'trusted, not checked' in a contest that is fundamentally visual.

ok.verdict: This design is inseparable from the torus—the track is a (2,3) trefoil knot that loops through both independent circuits, and the jump mechanic cuts across the tube interior to create a shortcut impossible on any flat track.
ok.evidence: The track is explicitly stated as a (2,3) torus knot winding twice around the ring and three times through the cross-section; the shift+space leap crosses the tube's interior to land on the opposite wall, which is a different part of the circuit, exploiting the torus's unique geometry and the corrected interior gravity field.
ok.strongest: Making the entire circuit a torus knot and then designing a jump that uses the interior tube gravity to create a racing shortcut that genuinely depends on the torus's shape.
ok.weakest: The 3D view is untested and unseen, so the claim that the whole knot is always hanging overhead—the torus's main visual affordance—is trusted but unverified, risking the 'make it look good' aim.

ok.verdict: The notes are exemplary in honesty: they clearly separate machine-verified facts, screenshot-verified 2D elements, and explicitly disclaim any visual verification of the 3D render, naming exactly what was inferred versus observed. No marketing gloss or overclaiming appears; the tradeoffs are stated as committed design choices with reasoning, not as achievements.
ok.evidence: The 'What's honest' section explicitly says 'Not verified: the 3D view... its look is trusted, not checked,' and it names real bugs found by instrumentation (offscreen-canvas backing store loss, virtualised rAF timestamps), which is the opposite of claiming more than it could know.
ok.strongest: The decision to clear the board and commit to a pure tube racer, explaining why a maze on a torus is a weak use of the geometry and making the trefoil knot the central affordance, is a bold, coherent choice that directly answers the brief's 'choose, commit' requirement.
ok.weakest: The claim that 'the whole knot is always visible' and 'you can read three corners ahead' is an untested visual/experiential assertion presented as design fact rather than a hypothesis, given the author admits they never saw the rendered 3D view.

ok.verdict: Real idea, genuinely committed: the diff actually deletes the maze generator, pellets, lives, score, ghost AI and the physics panel, and replaces them with a single argued conceit — a v=u spiral ribbon that makes one lap traverse the entire tube, over the top and through the inner equator. Ambition is concentrated in that move and in the race-against-yourself loop; it thins out at the visuals, which are a cautious re-skin of the shipped renderer defended after the fact as 'restraint.'
ok.evidence: `ribbonCenterY` is one line (c = x·WORLD_H/WORLD_W) that closes seamlessly and turns the torus topology into the course itself — the notes' 'minimum change that makes the topology the point rather than the backdrop' is borne out in code, not just prose. The ghost system (`bestTraj`, 'the second lap is always a race against the first', 'the reward for a clean lap is a faster ghost to chase') gives a self-escalating difficulty loop with zero AI opponents. Lap validation requires crossing the chequer on the ribbon, boost pads sit on the racing line so wobbling misses them, and the assist yields to input — all coherent consequences of the one idea. Hedging check: keeping the yellow palette and calling the rival ghost 'Pac-Man DNA' is a vestige, not a hedge; nothing of the maze game survives.
ok.strongest: The v=u ribbon: one closed curve that crosses every poloidal orientation once per lap, so the whole circuit is the whole tube and — because you're inside it — most of the track is visible ahead of you wrapped overhead. It's the rare design move where one equation generates the course, the spectacle, the minimap, and the difficulty curve (the claustrophobic inner equator as the fast, scary sector), and it answers 'why does this need to be inside a torus' rather than treating the torus as scenery.
ok.weakest: The 3D look: they kept the shipped SDF ray-marcher and lighting model essentially intact ('same SDF, same lighting model'), added surface dressing (kerbs, chevrons, fog), and framed the conservatism as restraint — on the one axis of the brief ('make it look good') where they admit they could verify nothing beyond geometry. The steering assist is the more contested choice, but it's at least an argued, owned compromise with a skill model built around it; the visual play-it-safe is where ambition was spent least.

ok.verdict: The diff is a cohesive, from-scratch rewrite that commits cleanly to the racing direction; the code is organized, the physics fix is elegant, and every tradeoff is stated.
ok.evidence: The replacement of the entire game logic, tile enum, steering assist math, metric-correct movement, and lap/ghost system, alongside the careful fallback import of field.mjs for the gravity fix, shows deliberate craft.
ok.strongest: The steering assist that yields to player input and enables a real autostart lap without sacrificing skill depth.
ok.weakest: The ghost replay is hardcoded to a single rival, not extensible to multiple ghosts.

ok.verdict: This design cannot be lifted onto a flat oval: the entire course is a (1,1) torus knot — one ribbon that winds once around the ring and once around the tube per lap — so both independent cycles of the torus are the track itself, and the interior does real work (you drive upside down on the ceiling, the rival ghost is visible across the tube, the racing line steepens at the inner equator because the metric says so). It is the canonical torus answer rather than a reskinned oval, though it uses the topology as a prescribed rail rather than a space offering route choice.
ok.evidence: ribbonCenterY(x) = x*WORLD_H/WORLD_W builds v=u, closing seamlessly after one lap; ribbonHeading(v) = atan2(r, R + r*cos(v)) bakes the torus metric into the steering line so the inner equator genuinely drives differently; the fixed analytic field makes 'down' the wall everywhere (ceiling driving is intrinsic, not visual); buildGhostData's comment 'if ghost is far, still show it (whole tube visible)' exploits interior sightlines; the jump integrates cross-section flight with the csR<0 → uTotal += π axis-crossing case, i.e. the tube volume is traversed, not just the surface. I am inferring (not observing) that the overhead-track spectacle lands, since the author states the WebGPU view was never seen headlessly — geometry was verified via a CPU ray-march, not appearance.
ok.strongest: Committing the whole course to the single v=u spiral with metric-correct movement: one decision that simultaneously forces both torus cycles into every lap, makes the inner equator a physically distinct stretch (shorter circumference, steeper line), and turns the whole tube into visible, meaningful track.
ok.weakest: Declaring everything off the ribbon to be mud: the second cycle is only ever experienced where the track prescribes it, so ~90% of the torus surface is scenery/penalty and the topology never offers a strategic choice (no viable cut, no alternate line using the inner equator's shorter path) — the one volume-using mechanic, the jump, is peripheral and even disabled under file://.

ok.verdict: The notes are transparent and meticulously honest, never claiming to have seen what the headless environment couldn't show. Tradeoffs are real, the boundaries of verification are explicit, and there is no marketing spin.
ok.evidence: The author explicitly writes: 'So I never saw the 3D view, and I am not going to claim I did.' They then list only things they could verify (gates, CPU ray-marcher geometry, racing simulation) and mark the visual result as 'trusting, unverified'.
ok.strongest: The clear separation of verified facts (scoring, pipeline init, rasterized geometry) from the unverified aesthetic claim, plus the honest note about the file:// CORS workaround and its effect on jump physics.
ok.weakest: The trust placed in the shader model and colour palette delivering a good 3D look is the biggest unknown, but it's fully acknowledged as unverified, so it doesn't undermine the notes' honesty.

ok.verdict: This is a design driven by a clear vision—transforming the torus interior into a racing line that only that topology could support—not a checklist, and the commit to a pure racer is total and defended with purpose.
ok.evidence: The racing line is a sine wave that snakes across both loops of the torus, the boost-hop lets you cut across the interior to shortcut a wave crest (a move a flat track cannot have), and the HUD gap counter explicitly ties the race to seeing the rival on the far wall overhead—all choices that exploit the geometry rather than just clearing the old maze.
ok.strongest: The decision to build a track that winds around both dimensions of the torus (u and v) turns steering into a real skill mechanic with apex cutting and a topology-dependent shortcut, immediately making the racing feel native to the world.
ok.weakest: The rival ghost's speed is driven by a sinusoidal script rather than an opponent that reads the track or adapts; it functions but lacks the design ambition shown elsewhere, especially next to the player's own best-lap ghost.

ok.verdict: This is a coherent rewrite with a single thesis, not a bolt-on: the maze/pellet/LUT/slider machinery is fully excised rather than stranded, the race systems (lap accounting, rival, best-lap ghost with wrap-aware interpolation) share one small set of documented constants, and every consequential tradeoff — uniform-magnitude gravity, u-progress speed, the file:// Blob fallback — is stated plainly in the notes and in code comments where a maintainer would trip over it. I'd maintain this; the honesty about what was verified versus trusted is itself a craft signal.
ok.evidence: The gravity fix replaces ~90 lines of numerically-integrated electrostatic LUT with a five-line analytic radial field whose invariants (sign, direction, uniformity, finiteness on the centreline) hold by construction, and the deletion is total — generateMaze, pellet rendering in WGSL, the physics panel and its seven slider listeners all go. Lap/ghost code shows real care: circSigned/circDist wrap handling in ghost interpolation, forward-only lap progress, blur/pointerlock key-clearing, and a guarded requestPointerLock. The disclosed warts are the tell: FIELD_SOURCE is a hand-synced byte-copy of field.mjs embedded as a string, LINE_MEAN is duplicated as a magic fraction in WGSL, and the aiSteer comment claims it's 'shared by the demo driver and the rival' when updateRival actually follows idealVRad directly — small drift between comment and code.
ok.strongest: Replacing the buggy LUT with the analytic statement of the intended field, and stating the tradeoff (uniform magnitude sacrifices realism for a fair race) as a deliberate design decision rather than discovering it later — the bug fix and the game design reinforce each other instead of being two separate patches.
ok.weakest: The FIELD_SOURCE hand-synced duplicate inside index.html: a byte-identical copy kept in sync 'by hand' is exactly the kind of thing that silently drifts, and it doubles down on the same pattern with LINE_MEAN/LINE_AMP re-derived as unexplained decimals in the shader; a tiny generation step or a single source of truth would have closed it.

ok.verdict: The design thoroughly exploits the torus geometry: the racing line winds around both loops, and the boost-hop cuts through the interior — impossible on a flat track. The rival appearing overhead on the far wall is a bonus that only a torus can offer.
ok.evidence: The ribbon circuit snakes across both torus directions, and the jump lets you shortcut through the doughnut hole, which a flat or cylindrical track can't replicate.
ok.strongest: The boost-hop shortcut through the interior of the torus, turning topology into a racing mechanic.
ok.weakest: The rival's visibility on the far wall is a cosmetic torus benefit that affects only the chase tension, not the core racing line.

ok.verdict: The notes are a model of epistemic discipline: they state plainly that the 3D view was never seen, bound every visual claim to what a shader compile plus texture readback can actually prove, and label their own abstractions as abstractions rather than realism. The few flourishes ('the honestest opponent there is', 'the strangest, most INPAC thing') are clearly rhetoric, not disguised verification claims, and every falsifiable number (422/1728, 0.0°, mean 87/stdev 56) is consistent with the machine results in front of me.
ok.evidence: The 'What I verified vs. what I'm trusting' section: 'The shader compile + readback prove it draws something structured, not that it looks good' — the author converts the headless-blindness constraint into explicit evidence limits instead of papering over it, and separately flags real tradeoffs (u-progress speed 'is an abstraction, not realism'; uniform gravity traded against physical plausibility; the byte-identical Blob copy 'kept in sync by hand').
ok.strongest: Refusing to claim the game looks good while still providing the strongest evidence a headless author can give (readback statistics, handedness check, lap-timing trace), and explicitly handing tone/composition/feel 'to you in the arena' — that is exactly the honesty the brief demanded.
ok.weakest: Minor: descriptions of aesthetic touches (the 'faint white breathing ghost', 'spectral cyan' rival) are written with present-tense confidence about on-screen effect; the code does assign those colors so it's a legitimate inference from source, but a half-sentence noting these are code-specified rather than seen would have made the discipline total.

ok.verdict: There is a real idea here and it is committed: they chose the maze race, argued it from the geometry itself (torus sightlines make pellets and ghost-lights readable at distance), and then deleted everything that contradicted the clock — lives, score, auto-run, physics panel. Ambition peaks early, though: one genuine inversion of racing orthodoxy, surrounded by disciplined but conservative simplification.
ok.evidence: The fork is declared and defended in the notes ('Why not a pure tube racer') and the diff follows through — the HUD is rebuilt around lap/best time, ghost contact becomes a +3s penalty with reset instead of a life, and the trade-away list shows no hedging. The standout line is 'Each lap regenerates a fresh maze… rewards adaptability, not memorisation,' which ties the race format to the one thing this geometry affords.
ok.strongest: Fresh procedurally-generated maze every lap with best-lap-time scoring — a time trial that tests routing and adaptation against the clock instead of track memorisation, a deliberate inversion of how racers normally work, and one that only makes sense inside a torus where you can read the far wall overhead. The ghost-as-penalty conversion is a close second: it preserves threat without run-ending failure, which is exactly how racing semantics should swallow Pac-Man lives.
ok.weakest: Gutting the physics toy: the Lorentz forces (B_CENTER, B_COIL) and the entire tuning panel are cut and the field is replaced by a hardcoded k=2.0 spring, justified only by 'not needed for feel.' Magnetically curved jumps were the original's weirdest verb; discarding them rather than retuning them for the race is the safe call dressed as a design call, and it flattens the game's strangeness to make the bug fix easy.

ok.verdict: The torus is genuinely load-bearing: the maze wraps both independent directions (wrapX/wrapY on u and v), the overhead far wall is used as live race information (pellets and ghost lights visible across the tube before you reach them), and the corrected spring field makes the entire interior wall a playable surface with ballistic jumps through the tube volume — this does not flatten onto an oval. But the race layer added on top is topology-agnostic: 'clear the board on a clock' would run identically on any closed maze, and no new mechanic exploits the two loops or the interior as a racing line.
ok.evidence: The notes explicitly justify keeping the maze by citing cross-tube sightlines as gameplay ('pellets are visible well before you reach them, and the ghost lights tell you where the chasers are'), which only holds inside a closed tube; the diff retains full cross-section jump ballistics (csR/csZ integration, landing on arbitrary wall v, csR<0 handling for crossing to the opposite side); and the gravity fix (g = k·(R−R0, Z), always toward the wall) is verified directionally at every interior sample, replacing the sign-reversing LUT. Against that: the lap definition is 'eat every pellet' with a freshly regenerated maze each lap, and no race primitive references torus structure — I'm inferring the sightline and jump-shortcut value from code and notes, since nobody can see the render headlessly.
ok.strongest: Committing to the maze race precisely because the torus interior is the affordance — preserving the renderer where the far wall curves overhead and turning that visibility into race-relevant information, while the analytic interior gravity makes wall-down exact everywhere so the whole tube (not just the floor strip) stays playable at speed.
ok.weakest: The race design adds nothing torus-native of its own: laps are full board clears on regenerated layouts, which discards route knowledge and treats the surface as interchangeable with any closed maze — no cross-tube jump lines as rewarded shortcuts, no use of the hole, no structure built on the two independent ways around; the torus is inherited scenery for the clock rather than the race's own design.

ok.verdict: The notes are mostly honest about the biggest limitation—they openly state that the 3D view is unverified—and they give real tradeoff reasoning. But they overclaim the gravity fix as being backed by `field.mjs` when the diff shows an inline function copy, so the notes vouch for something the entry does not actually contain.
ok.evidence: The 'What I could not verify' section is candid, but the gravity section and confirm list claim `field.mjs` exports and passes checks; the diff only defines a local `importedField()` in index.html and never imports a .mjs module.
ok.strongest: The explicit list of what could not be verified (3D render, HUD appearance, feel, lap transitions) avoids the main forbidden claim.
ok.weakest: The misleading `field.mjs`/inline-import framing is a trust-damaging inconsistency; it makes the reader unsure whether the physics checks were actually run on the shipped code.

ok.verdict: A real design, not a checklist: the lap is a full toroidal wrap, so the topology is the race track while the maze/pellets are the route; ghost hits as +3s time penalties are a coherent translation of survival tension into clock pressure. It commits firmly to the Pac-Man fork, though the optional auto-run that can drive itself and the admitted inability to verify fun make the final ambition partly speculative.
ok.evidence: Lap tracking uses cumulative forward x progress across WORLD_W, ghost collision adds 3 seconds and respawns instead of game over, and maze clear regenerates the maze without stopping the run.
ok.strongest: Defining a lap by one circumnavigation of the torus in u — it makes the torus's shape the race, not just a container.
ok.weakest: Explicitly leaving Ghost AI unchanged; ghosts became time penalties but behave exactly as in the original, so the racing conversion stops short of reimagining them as racing obstacles or traffic.

ok.verdict: Coherent, committed, and honestly documented — this reads like a PR from someone who deletes code with confidence: the LUT, Lorentz forces, physics sliders, lives, and score are all cleanly excised rather than left to rot, and the race layer (lap tracking, penalties, HUD, harness contract) is added in the same idiom as the existing code. It is not bug-free: the lap accumulator has a real correctness hole, but the overall structure is something I would maintain.
ok.evidence: The physics fix replaces ~100 lines of numerically-integrated gravity LUT with a single analytic call `field(absR, csZ, {R, r})`, with the field.js/field.mjs duplication explicitly justified (file:// CORS in headless Chromium) in both a code comment and the notes. But in `checkGhostCollision` the respawn teleports the player without resyncing `lastRawX`, so the next `updateRaceLaps` sees a huge dx that the wrap-around correction can flip positive — gifting up to ~half a lap of phantom forward progress per ghost hit; and the same penalty is applied as `raceElapsed += 3.0` (seconds) and `lapStartTime += 3000` (ms) on adjacent lines, a two-units-one-value smell.
ok.strongest: Subtractive discipline: every removed subsystem (LUT, B-fields, sliders, lives, game-over) is removed fully — call sites, listeners, DOM, and styles — and the notes state each tradeoff and each thing they could not verify, which is exactly the honesty a reviewer needs when the WebGPU output can't be observed headlessly.
ok.weakest: Lap accounting: counting only positive dx means oscillating back and forth also inflates progress, the respawn teleport feeds garbage into the accumulator, and there is no start/finish-line validation — the single mechanic that defines a race entry is its least rigorous code, and the notes don't acknowledge it.

ok.verdict: It uses the torus's long way around as the lap and keeps the maze wrapped in both directions, so it is not just a flat oval; but the second independent loop is never raced, so the torus's signature two-way topology is underused.
ok.evidence: updateRaceLaps counts only cumulative forward x-progress and wraps WORLD_W, with no poloidal/v-direction lap or scoring, so the race objective would survive almost unchanged on a flat loop.
ok.strongest: Committing to Pac-Man DNA and making a full u-direction circumnavigation the lap ties the race to the torus and preserves the maze identity.
ok.weakest: The v-direction (the second way around the torus) is reduced to a wrapped maze dimension rather than a raced or strategic element.

ok.verdict: The notes are scrupulously honest about epistemic limits: every checkable claim (the ±108° auto-run scan = code's ±0.6π, autostart heading +X = playerAngle π/2, physics checks = gate PASS) matches the diff, and the author explicitly refuses to claim anything about the WebGPU render they could not see. The one place the prose outruns the code is the penalty: raceElapsed and lapStartTime are both shifted +3s, so the penalty cancels out of lap timing — 'every hit costs you the lap' is asserted but not delivered — and the autostart-only CELL_UNIT=2 maze change is never disclosed.
ok.evidence: The 'What I couldn't verify' section: 'Headless Chromium does not composite the WebGPU surface into screenshots... I tuned it against the scoring contract, not against gameplay feel. The ghost penalty of 3 seconds is an untested number.' — admissions against interest, corroborated by the diff. Contrast with checkGhostCollision(): raceElapsed += 3.0 AND lapStartTime += 3000, so lapMs = raceElapsed*1000 - lapStartTime is invariant to hits, contradicting the notes' core tension claim; and the autostart block silently sets CELL_UNIT = 2, giving the harness a different maze density than a player gets.
ok.strongest: Declining all aesthetic claims — preserving the shader unchanged and saying only 'I trust it renders as it did before,' while enumerating exactly what the capture harness can confirm (HUD, minimap, clock) versus cannot (the 3D view). This is precisely the restraint the brief demanded, and the tradeoffs section (lives tension, geometry knobs, Lorentz jumps) names real losses rather than spinning them.
ok.weakest: Claiming 'the clock pressure replaces survival pressure: every hit costs you the lap' when the implementation makes lap times — the only recorded competitive metric — immune to ghost hits; as written, the optimal play is to plow through ghosts, and the notes present a designed consequence the code doesn't produce. The undisclosed autostart CELL_UNIT=2 tweak, paired with the admission of contract-tuning, is the runner-up.

ok.verdict: This is a committed, genuinely designed race game: clearing the maze in favor of a torus-knot ribbon course is a real spatial idea rather than a checklist item. The direction is stated plainly and the rework follows it consistently, with only a token Pac-Man ghost naming and a jump-as-flavour hedge holding it back.
ok.evidence: The notes explicitly choose pure tube racer, and the diff backs it up by deleting the maze/pellets/enemy-ghost machinery and replacing it with a (1,1) torus-knot racing line, eight gates, a best-lap ghost, and boost groove.
ok.strongest: Making the lap a (1,1) torus knot—one toroidal loop plus one poloidal wind—so the painted cyan line is literally the racing line and the whole course wraps overhead is the most interesting spatial decision.
ok.weakest: Keeping jump as 'flavour' rather than as a racing mechanic is the timid leftover: it adds a control input with no competitive consequence because gates only count grounded.

ok.verdict: The diff is a clean, coherent rewrite that surgically removes the maze and physics sliders for a focused tube racer, with well-structured race state, a deliberate analytical gravity fix, and a WebGPU renderer that fully exploits the torus interior. Tradeoffs are explicitly stated and the code is maintainable, though the monolithic HTML/JS could benefit from modularisation in the long term.
ok.evidence: The field.mjs import with a byte-identical inline fallback for file:// scoring, the clearly layered race state machine (countdown → racing → finished), and the shader that renders the racing line, gates, ghost, and survey grid — all carefully built around the (1,1) torus-knot track.
ok.strongest: Deliberately forking to a pure tube racer around a (1,1) curve, which turns the torus's unique geometry into the core gameplay loop, backed by the analytic gravity field that replaces the buggy LUT.
ok.weakest: The renderer lives in a single large inline shader string and the entire application is in one script block; while coherent, it would be harder to split into reusable modules if the project grew.

ok.verdict: This entry is built around the torus rather than merely set on it: the lap is a (1,1) torus knot that winds once poloidally per toroidal lap, and the first-person camera inside the tube is what makes the whole ribbon and gate sequence readable overhead. It could not work unchanged on a flat oval, because the inner-wall/outer-wall transition and the overhead wrap of the course are the race.
ok.evidence: The track model explicitly defines the racing line as v = u in the torus parameterisation, and the notes say a lap is a '(1,1) line on the tube wall,' taking the player across the outer wall, over the top, across the inner wall, and under the bottom — a true use of both torus cycles.
ok.strongest: Committing to a pure tube racer and making the racing line itself a torus knot, so the torus topology is not decoration but the course.
ok.weakest: The two independent ways around the torus are combined into one predetermined groove rather than offered as route choices; the gates are toroidally spaced arches that check the line, so the poloidal winding is scenic and navigational but never a real branching decision.

ok.verdict: The notes are refreshingly honest: they clearly separate what was verified headlessly from what was not, admit untested hardware performance, and detail real tradeoffs like junking the maze and sliders.
ok.evidence: They state 'Not verified: how it looks on a real GPU. This sandbox kills any sustained WebGPU session ... For that reason the renderer ships with serialized GPU work, adaptive resolution ... and a 2D unwrapped-track fallback.' They list exactly what they checked (scoring, race logic via sim, frame readback with debug snapshot) without pretending to see it on a real display.
ok.strongest: Transparency about the adaptive resolution fallback and the deliberately shipped debug hooks, showing they prioritized robustness over false claims.
ok.weakest: The mention of 'caught numerically, fixed, re-verified' for the WGSL error is slightly vague about what numerical check was done, but overall it’s still well within the bounds of what they could know from frame readback.
